c4581202dd.q: How did Dean Salakas become Australia's first click and collect retailer in 1999?
c4581202dd.a: While in high school in 1999, Dean Salakas launched The Party People business online, which made it Australia's first retailer to offer click and collect functionality. He later discovered Google AdWords coming to Australia in 2003 during a university project and became Google AdWords' first advertiser, paying one cent per click.
c4581202dd.e: S2 Ep23: The Retail Shift: Exploring the changing landscape of Australian retail with Dean Salakas

fc295252c3.q: What is the key difference between how The Party People positioned itself versus competitors?
fc295252c3.a: Dean positioned The Party People not as a business selling party products, but as a business helping people have the parties they dream about. He explains: 'Everyone thought they were in the business of selling party products. I looked at it that I was in the business of helping people have parties.' This distinction influenced every strategic decision, including offering services that don't make money but help customers have parties.
fc295252c3.e: S2 Ep23: The Retail Shift: Exploring the changing landscape of Australian retail with Dean Salakas

70fd3f7d2d.q: How many members does the Australian retail community WhatsApp group have that Dean Salakas built?
70fd3f7d2d.a: Dean started a WhatsApp chat with Jethro Marks at a conference to organize drinks. The chat group grew to 100 people by the end of the first day, 300 by the end of the conference, and now has 4,000+ members 18 months later, becoming his primary focus.
70fd3f7d2d.e: S2 Ep23: The Retail Shift: Exploring the changing landscape of Australian retail with Dean Salakas

38f5d85b1b.q: What role do robots play in inventory management at major Australian retailers like Kmart and Bunnings?
38f5d85b1b.a: Robots that look like RoboVacs with a pole on top are now counting inventory in stores at Kmart and Bunnings. These robots look at inventory levels on every shelf and perform inventory counts every night, effectively replacing stock takers in these stores.
38f5d85b1b.e: S2 Ep23: The Retail Shift: Exploring the changing landscape of Australian retail with Dean Salakas

42eab59bbb.q: How did The Party People differentiate its in-store experience from competitors?
42eab59bbb.a: Customers walking into The Party People were immediately hit with a 'wow factor.' The store had balloons everywhere, decorations, and displays packed to the roof at eight meters high, making the space visually appealing. Dean explains: 'People judge you on your first five seconds like a person. The store's the same. They judge you as soon as they walk in.' This immediate visual impact created a strong first impression.
42eab59bbb.e: S2 Ep23: The Retail Shift: Exploring the changing landscape of Australian retail with Dean Salakas

7142f4fb59.q: What are the main challenges small retailers face competing against Amazon, Shein, and Temu in Australia?
7142f4fb59.a: Dean says buying customers through digital advertising is difficult as a primary strategy, though it should be part of the mix. The real answer is having an amazing product that solves a customer problem better than anyone else, combined with making noise about what you do through media and PR. He emphasizes: 'You've got to have a great product that solves a problem. And you've got to make sure everyone knows about it. And you can't have one without the other.'
7142f4fb59.e: S2 Ep23: The Retail Shift: Exploring the changing landscape of Australian retail with Dean Salakas
